# Setup

The flowcharts in this notebook are Mermaid diagrams written by R code.
The trees visible when the page opens are drawn by Quarto; those inside tabs are drawn by a small script the first time their tab is opened, because a diagram in a hidden tab cannot be laid out (see `code/00_helper/pid_tree.R`).

```{r}
#| label: setup

# To track render duration
start_time <- Sys.time()

# set width of console output
options(width = 80)


# Install and load required packages
p_required <- c(
  "tidyverse",
  "here",
  "sessioninfo"
)
packages <- rownames(installed.packages())
p_to_install <- p_required[!(p_required %in% packages)]
if (length(p_to_install) > 0) {
  install.packages(p_to_install)
}
sapply(p_required, require, character.only = TRUE)
rm(p_required, p_to_install, packages)

# Shared tree helpers
source(here("code", "00_helper", "pid_tree.R"))

# Party Facts helpers and the alias, alliance and lineage tables of notebook 1.9
source(here("code", "00_helper", "pf_code.R"))
rules <- pf_rules()
```

# The Tree

Every composition notebook (2.1 to 2.4) sorts respondents into the same sequential tree, following the typology in the notes of `index.qmd`.
The levels follow the order in which the questionnaire asked the items (each notebook's *Question Order* section).
Where the vote came before the attachment item, the tree splits on the vote first; where the attachment came first, on the attachment first.
A tree that pools waves or studies with different orders (only the CSES has any) uses the order of most of its respondents.

- **Vote.** Does the respondent report a party vote?
  *No vote reported* collects non-voters, blank or invalid ballots, don't know, refusals and missing answers, and "other" votes whose open text names no party.
  Where a survey wave never asked the vote item, the branch reads *vote item not fielded* instead, so that "not asked" is not confused with "did not answer".
- **Attachment.** Does the respondent report feeling close to a party?
  The answer is *yes* (a party is named), *no*, or *don't know / refused / missing*.
  The last group gets its own grey box so that the shares at every level add up to 100%.
  An "other" answer counts as *yes* only if its open text names a real party (see [Other Answers](#other-answers)).
- **Leaner probe.** Where the survey follows a *no* or *don't know* with *do you feel yourself a little closer to one of the political parties than the others?* (the CSES and the EES 2009 wave), those respondents split into *leaner*, *not leaning*, and a grey *probe DK* box.
  Leaner boxes have a dashed green border.
  Where a tree pools surveys with and without the probe, the respondents who never got it sit in a grey *probe not fielded* box.
- **Match.** Only for respondents who report a vote and name a party (attached or leaner), the two parties are compared by their Party Facts coding with the rule of notebook 1.9: *same party* when they are the same party, one is an alias of the other, one is an electoral alliance or joint list that contains the other, or one continued in the other through a rename, refoundation or merger (from the year of the succession on); *different party* otherwise, including two members of one alliance, two predecessors of one successor, and a breakaway and its parent.
  Because both sides are always a named party, no respondent in this notebook is *not matchable*.

The leaves named after the typology are *explicit partisan* (attached, same party), *leaner* (leaner, same party), **vote-anchored** (vote reported, no attachment, and not a leaner where the probe was asked; the data files call it *implicit*), and *non-partisan* (no vote, no attachment, not a leaner).
Vote-anchored respondents are not leaners: leaners come from the attitudinal probe, the vote-anchored from the vote.

Every box gives the number of respondents, and every arrow gives the share of the box above it.
The two groups the contrast rests on are filled in the colours of the figures: the *explicit partisans* (attachment reported, vote for the same party) in dark blue, the *vote-anchored* (attachment denied, vote reported) in dark orange.
The arrows leading to them are drawn thick in the same colours, and in black where a path leads to both.
The figures use one colour family per kind of answer: blues for attached respondents, greens for leaners, oranges for neither, greys for DK and not fielded, stacked in that order.

# Load Data

The source is the published harmonised release, not the old analysis frame in `data/03_final/`.
As in notebook 1.8, only respondents who passed the attention check (`der_att_check_3`) are kept.

```{r}
#| label: load-eu25-data

eu25games <- read_rds(
  here(
    "data",
    "01_raw",
    "eu25games2019.rds"
  )
) |>
  # Attention-check passers, as in 1.8
  filter(der_att_check_3)
```

# Question Order

Every item about turnout, vote choice and party attachment, in the order a respondent saw them.
The source is the Irish English version of each wave's Qualtrics questionnaire (`data/questionaire/W{1,2,3}_EU25_Survey_Ireland_basic.pdf` in the `eu25games2019` repository); the release variable is from its `variable_crosswalk.csv`.
Qualtrics numbers questions by creation, not by display, so the order below is the display order of the printed flow (in wave 3, `Q52` comes after `Q54`--`Q56`).
The survey is online and self-completed in every wave.

```{r}
#| label: items

items <- tribble(
  ~wave, ~pos, ~question, ~variable, ~role, ~wording, ~asked,
  # Wave 1
  1, 1, "Q61", "q_eu_vote_2014", "vote intention (EP 2019)",
  "On Friday, May 24th 2019, the European election takes place. All citizens of the European Union elect the members of the European Parliament. Which party will you vote for? [not eligible / will not vote / parties / other / don't know]",
  "all; asked right after the EU text of a priming experiment (Q61, Q64, Q67 or Q69 by arm)",
  1, 2, "Q75", "q_party_id", "attachment and party",
  "Do you consider yourself to be close to any particular political party? If so, which party do you feel close to? [parties / other / No, I do not feel close to any political party]",
  "all; asked right after the text of a second priming experiment (Q75, Q80, Q85 or Q89 by arm)",
  1, 3, "Q76", "q_party_closeness", "strength",
  "Do you feel yourself to be very close to this party, fairly close, or merely a sympathiser?",
  "if a party or other named",
  # Wave 2
  2, 1, "Q42", "q_vote_turnout_likelihood", "turnout",
  "On Friday, 24 May 2019, the European election takes place. [...] How likely is it that you will vote in the upcoming election? [not eligible / certain not to ... certain to vote / have already voted / don't know]",
  "all",
  2, 2, "Q43", "q_vote_turnout_confirm", "turnout check",
  "Just to be clear, we are recording that you already voted in the election [...]. Is that right?",
  "if already voted",
  2, 3, "Q44", "q_vote_choice_past", "vote cast (EP 2019)",
  "Which party did you give your 1st preference vote to in this election?",
  "if confirmed as voted",
  2, 4, "Q45", "q_vote_choice_intended", "vote intention (EP 2019)",
  "Which party will you give your 1st preference vote in this election?",
  "if might, likely or certain to vote",
  2, 5, "Q46", "q_vote_choice_hypo", "hypothetical vote (EP 2019)",
  "Just assuming you were going to vote in the election, which party would you give your 1st preference vote?",
  "if not eligible, unlikely or certain not to vote, or don't know",
  2, 6, "Q51", "q_vote_choice_past2014", "previous vote (EP 2014)",
  "This question is about the previous European Parliament elections that were held five years ago. Which party did you give your 1st preference vote in the previous European Parliament elections in 2014?",
  "all",
  2, 7, "Q52", "q_party_id", "attachment and party",
  "Do you consider yourself to be close to any particular political party? If so, which party do you feel close to?",
  "all; no strength item",
  # Wave 3
  3, 1, "Q53", "q_vote_turnout_likelihood", "turnout",
  "European Parliament elections were held on Friday, 24 May 2019. For one reason or another, some people in Ireland did not vote in these elections. [...] Which of the following statements best describes you? [not eligible / did not vote / thought about voting / usually vote but didn't / I am sure I voted]",
  "all",
  3, 2, "Q54", "q_vote_choice_past", "vote cast (EP 2019)",
  "Which party did you give your 1st preference vote to in this election?",
  "if sure they voted",
  3, 3, "Q55", "q_vote_choice_hypo", "hypothetical vote (EP 2019)",
  "Just assuming you had voted in the election, which party would you have voted for?",
  "if not voted or not eligible",
  3, 4, "Q56", "q_vote_choice_past2014", "previous vote (EP 2014)",
  "This question is about the previous European Parliament elections that were held five years ago. [...]",
  "all",
  3, 5, "Q52", "q_party_id", "attachment and party",
  "Do you consider yourself to be close to any particular political party? If so, which party do you feel close to?",
  "all; no strength item"
)

items |>
  select(Wave = wave, `#` = pos, Question = question, Variable = variable, Role = role, Wording = wording, `Asked of` = asked) |>
  knitr::kable()

# Vote before attachment, per wave
item_order <- items |>
  summarise(
    vote_first = min(pos[str_detect(role, "EP 2019")]) <
      min(pos[str_detect(role, "attachment")]),
    .by = wave
  )
item_order
```

In order:

- **Wave 1:** Q61 → Q75 → Q76
- **Wave 2:** Q42 → Q43 → Q44 / Q45 / Q46 → Q51 → Q52
- **Wave 3:** Q53 → Q54 / Q55 → Q56 → Q52

The vote comes before the attachment item in all three waves, so every tree below splits on the vote first.
Some differences matter for a comparison:

- **The vote changes meaning across waves.** Wave 1 asks a pure intention months before the election; wave 2 routes respondents to a cast vote, an intention or a hypothetical vote depending on their turnout answer; wave 3 asks a cast vote or a hypothetical one.
  The hypothetical vote is asked of non-voters and counts as a reported vote below (as in the old pipeline).
- **The previous EP vote (2014)** sits between the 2019 vote and the attachment item in waves 2 and 3, so the attachment item follows two party-choice questions there and one in wave 1.
- **Priming.** In wave 1 both the vote and the attachment item come right after an experimental text about the EU, whose content varies by arm.
- **Strength** of attachment is asked only in wave 1.
- **The French wave-2 questionnaire** is a separate version with its own items (`q_party_id_fra` and friends), folded in below.
- The attachment item names the party in the same step (no separate yes/no filter), and there is no leaner probe.

# Select Attachment and Vote Items

The attachment item is the EES wording -- *do you consider yourself to be close to any particular political party? If so, which party do you feel close to?* -- asked in all three waves.
French respondents in wave 2 answered a separate French version of every party item (`q_party_id_fra` and friends), so those columns are coalesced into the main ones.

The vote item concerns the **European Parliament election of May 2019** in all three waves.
Wave 1 asks the intended vote (`Q61`). The release names this item `q_eu_vote_2014`, but the question is about the 2019 election.
Wave 2 was fielded around the election and asks for the intended vote, the vote already cast, or a hypothetical vote; wave 3 asks for the vote cast or a hypothetical vote.
The wave-2 and wave-3 items are coalesced in the order intention, hypothetical, past -- the recall-maximising rule of the old pipeline (`code/02_key_variables/2.1_key_variables.qmd`, commit `4651e2c`).
The questionnaire routes each respondent to only one of them by their turnout answer (see [Question Order](#question-order)).

Every party answer comes with a Party Facts name (`ext_*_pf_name`).
Non-party answers carry a literal sentinel string instead, and parties missing from Party Facts are marked `[og]` -- those are real parties and are kept as such.
So the sentinel strings are matched literally rather than by testing for a missing Party Facts ID.

```{r}
#| label: sentinels

# Non-party answers in Party Facts
pf_no_party <- c(
  "none",
  "dont-know",
  "refused",
  "did-not-vote",
  "will-not-vote",
  "blank-invalid",
  "not-eligible"
)

# Named, but not a codeable party
pf_other <- c("other", "other-country", "independent")

# Sentinels actually present
eu25games |>
  transmute(
    pid = coalesce(ext_q_party_id_pf_name, ext_q_party_id_fra_pf_name)
  ) |>
  filter(pid %in% c(pf_no_party, pf_other) | is.na(pid)) |>
  count(pid)
```

The attachment item has no don't-know code.
A respondent either names a party, says "none", or leaves it empty; the empty answers are what the grey *DK / missing* box counts.

## Other Answers {#other-answers}

Every party item offers an "other" option with an open text field (`q_*_other_raw`; `q_eu_vote_2014_raw_text` for the wave-1 vote), and the release codes that text to Party Facts as well (`ext_q_*_other_pf_name`; `ext_q_eu_vote_2014_text_pf_name`).
An "other" answer is replaced by what its open text says, so that it counts as attachment or vote only if the text names a real party:

- **A real party:** the party is used, for the tree level and for the match.
  This includes parties Party Facts does not list, which the release marks `[og]`.
- **A clear denial:** *no attachment*, and *no vote reported* on the vote item.
- **Anything else** (don't know, refusal, several parties, a political camp, an independent candidate, junk): *DK / missing* on the attachment item, *no vote reported* on the vote item.

The release codes most open texts, but not all: about half of the open attachment answers and most open vote answers carry no code at all, among them plain party names ("Aontu", "Mislav Kolakušić", "Δημιουργία Ξανά").
These are coded by hand below, from a reading of every uncoded text.

- `other_text_parties` maps a text to a party.
  Where the release already uses a name for that party in that country, the same name is used, so that an attachment and a vote for the same party match.
  A party that appears nowhere else gets a new name ending in `[hand]`.
  A text counts only if it names one party: a party's name or abbreviation (also misspelt or transliterated), its leader, or a candidate on its list.
  Ambiguous abbreviations are left out.
- `other_denials` lists the attachment texts that say the respondent is close to no party.
  Complaints about parties, "a bit of several" and undecided answers do not count.
  The vote item needs no such list, because a denial and anything else both end in *no vote reported*.

```{r}
# One party per text
stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(other_text_parties[c("country", "text")]))

# Replace an "other" answer by what its open text says
resolve_other <- function(answer, other_pf, text, country, denials = character()) {
  text <- str_squish(text)
  hand <- other_text_parties$party[match(
    paste(country, text),
    paste(other_text_parties$country, other_text_parties$text)
  )]
  case_when(
    !answer %in% pf_other ~ answer,
    # Coded upstream to a party or non-party answer
    !is.na(other_pf) & !other_pf %in% pf_other ~ other_pf,
    !is.na(hand) ~ hand,
    text %in% denials ~ "none",
    # Anything else stays "other"
    .default = "other"
  )
}
```

```{r}
#| label: select-vars

eu25_tree <- eu25games |>
  transmute(
    meta_responseid,
    wave = meta_wave,
    country_name = meta_country,
    # French wave-2 items folded in
    pid_answer = coalesce(ext_q_party_id_pf_name, ext_q_party_id_fra_pf_name),
    pid_other_pf = coalesce(
      ext_q_party_id_other_pf_name,
      ext_q_party_id_other_fra_pf_name
    ),
    pid_other_text = coalesce(q_party_id_other_raw, q_party_id_other_fra_raw),
    pid = resolve_other(
      pid_answer,
      pid_other_pf,
      pid_other_text,
      meta_country,
      denials = other_denials
    ),
    # The "other" answer behind the vote
    vote_answer = coalesce(
      ext_q_eu_vote_2014_pf_name,
      ext_q_vote_choice_intended_pf_name,
      ext_q_vote_choice_hypo_pf_name,
      ext_q_vote_choice_past_pf_name,
      ext_q_vote_choice_hypo_fra_pf_name,
      ext_q_vote_choice_past_fra_pf_name
    ),
    # Wave-1 intention; then intention, hypothetical, past
    vote_party = coalesce(
      resolve_other(
        ext_q_eu_vote_2014_pf_name,
        ext_q_eu_vote_2014_text_pf_name,
        q_eu_vote_2014_raw_text,
        meta_country
      ),
      resolve_other(
        ext_q_vote_choice_intended_pf_name,
        ext_q_vote_choice_intended_other_pf_name,
        q_vote_choice_intended_other_raw,
        meta_country
      ),
      resolve_other(
        ext_q_vote_choice_hypo_pf_name,
        ext_q_vote_choice_hypo_other_pf_name,
        q_vote_choice_hypo_other_raw,
        meta_country
      ),
      resolve_other(
        ext_q_vote_choice_past_pf_name,
        ext_q_vote_choice_past_other_pf_name,
        q_vote_choice_past_other_raw,
        meta_country
      ),
      resolve_other(
        ext_q_vote_choice_hypo_fra_pf_name,
        ext_q_vote_choice_hypo_other_fra_pf_name,
        q_vote_choice_hypo_other_fra_raw,
        meta_country
      ),
      resolve_other(
        ext_q_vote_choice_past_fra_pf_name,
        ext_q_vote_choice_past_other_fra_pf_name,
        q_vote_choice_past_other_fra_raw,
        meta_country
      )
    )
  )

# Every hand-coded text found
open_texts <- eu25games |>
  select(
    country_name = meta_country,
    matches("^q_(party_id|vote_choice_(intended|hypo|past))_other(_fra)?_raw$"),
    q_eu_vote_2014_raw_text
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(-country_name, values_to = "text") |>
  mutate(text = str_squish(text)) |>
  filter(!is.na(text))
stopifnot(
  all(other_denials %in% open_texts$text),
  all(
    paste(other_text_parties$country, other_text_parties$text) %in%
      paste(open_texts$country_name, open_texts$text)
  )
)

# Names reused from the release exist in it
pf_names <- eu25games |>
  select(matches("^ext_q_(party_id|vote_choice|eu_vote_2014).*_pf_name$")) |>
  unlist(use.names = FALSE) |>
  unique()
reused <- other_text_parties |>
  filter(!str_ends(party, fixed("[hand]")))
stopifnot(all(reused$party %in% pf_names))

# How "other" answers resolve
resolution <- function(resolved, other_pf) {
  case_when(
    resolved %in% c(pf_no_party, pf_other) ~ resolved,
    !is.na(other_pf) & !other_pf %in% pf_other ~ "party (coded)",
    .default = "party (by hand)"
  )
}
eu25_tree |>
  filter(pid_answer %in% pf_other) |>
  count(attachment = resolution(pid, pid_other_pf))
eu25_tree |>
  filter(vote_answer %in% pf_other) |>
  count(vote = case_when(
    vote_party %in% c(pf_no_party, pf_other) ~ vote_party,
    .default = "party"
  ))
```

```{r}
      "Lithuania" ~ "LT",
      "Netherlands" ~ "NL",
      "Poland" ~ "PL",
      "Portugal" ~ "PT",
      "Romania" ~ "RO",
      "Slovakia" ~ "SK",
      "Slovenia" ~ "SI",
      "Spain" ~ "ES",
      "Sweden" ~ "SE",
      "United Kingdom" ~ "GB"
    ),
    # Level 1: attachment, uncoded other as DK
    att = case_when(
      is.na(pid) | pid %in% c("dont-know", "refused", pf_other) ~ "dk",
      pid %in% pf_no_party ~ "no",
      .default = "yes"
    ),
    # Level 2: vote, asked in every wave
    vote = case_when(
      is.na(vote_party) | vote_party %in% c(pf_no_party, pf_other) ~ "no",
      .default = "yes"
    ),
    # Level 3: same Party Facts party, with aliases, alliances and lineage
    # (notebook 1.9); all waves were fielded in 2019
    match = case_when(
      att != "yes" | vote != "yes" ~ NA,
      .default = pf_match(country, pid, vote_party, rules, 2019L)
    ),
    route = if_else(match == "same", pf_match_route(country, pid, vote_party, rules, 2019L), NA),
    # Tree order from the questionnaire
    vote_first = item_order$vote_first[match(wave, item_order$wave)],
    wave = factor(paste("Wave", wave))
  ) |>
  select(meta_responseid, wave, country, att, vote, match, route, pid, vote_party, vote_first)

# Every country mapped
stopifnot(all(eu25_tree$country %in% countries_25))
```

# Checks

The raw answers behind each tree level, printed so that any unexpected code is visible.
The first table crosses the three levels by wave, the second lists the most frequent attachment/vote pairs that end up as *different party*, and the third the pairs that are the *same party* only through an alias, an alliance or lineage (the audit trail of the tables of notebook 1.9).

```{r}
#| label: checks

# Levels by wave
eu25_tree |>
  count(wave, att, vote, match) |>
  print(n = Inf)

# Most common mismatches
eu25_tree |>
  filter(match == "different") |>
  count(country, pid, vote_party, sort = TRUE) |>
  slice_head(n = 15)

# Same party through a table, by route
eu25_tree |>
  filter(route %in% c("alias", "alliance", "lineage")) |>
  count(route, country, pid, vote_party, sort = TRUE) |>
  mutate(across(c(pid, vote_party), \(x) str_trunc(x, 40))) |>
  print(n = 40)
```

The unit here is the **respondent-wave**, not the person.
The panel re-interviews part of the sample, so a respondent who took part in two waves is counted twice in the pooled tree, and the attachment item may be answered differently each time.
Attention-check passers also include a few within-wave duplicates of the same panelist, which the published frame does not remove.

```{r}
#| label: panel-structure

# Waves per panelist
eu25games |>
  count(meta_pid, name = "rows") |>
  count(rows, name = "panelists")
```

# Leaner Probes

The eu25games questionnaire carries no leaner probe, so no tree in this notebook has a leaner level.
The only follow-up to the attachment item is its strength (`q_party_closeness`), asked in wave 1 of those who name a party (see [Question Order](#question-order)).

# Caveats

- **The vote is a European Parliament vote**: an intention in wave 1, and in wave 2 mostly an intended or hypothetical one.
  Comparing it with a national-election recall in the CSES and ESS notebooks means comparing different quantities.
- **The release's name for the wave-1 vote is misleading.** `q_eu_vote_2014` holds the 2019 vote intention (`Q61`), not a 2014 vote.
- **Hand-coded "other" answers.** Open texts the release left uncoded are coded by hand (see [Other Answers](#other-answers)), which is a judgement call for short or misspelt texts.
  A party that appears only in hand-coded texts carries a `[hand]` name, so an attachment to it can only match a vote that was hand-coded as well.
  Votes for independent candidates count as *no vote reported*, and attachment to them as *DK / missing*.
- **Respondent-waves, not persons.** See the panel table above.
- **Matching is by Party Facts party, with aliases, alliances and lineage** (notebook 1.9), in all four composition notebooks alike. A party and an electoral alliance containing it count as the *same party* (Fidesz and the Fidesz–KDNP list, Civic Platform and the European Coalition, Podemos and Unidas Podemos); so do a party and the party it continued in through a rename, refoundation or merger, from the year of the succession on; and the release's own labels for a listed party (the PvdA's EP list label, "Spring" for Wiosna) are aliases of it.
  Two members of one alliance (PLUS and USR in 2019, two years before they merged), two predecessors of one successor, a breakaway and its parent, and `[hand]` parties outside the tables stay *different party*; genuine switches (e.g. Conservative attachment, Brexit Party vote in Britain) stay as they are. The `route` column records which table made a pair the same party.
- **Panel duplicates.** A handful of panelists appear many times over (one 29 times), which the attention-check filter does not remove.
  Notebook 3.1 removes them for the analysis data.

# Save

The tree frame, one row per respondent-wave, is the partisan classification the analysis notebooks build on (notebook 3.1 joins it by `meta_responseid`).

```{r}
#| label: save-partisan

# Row key is unique
stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(eu25_tree$meta_responseid))

eu25_tree |>
  mutate(wave = as.integer(str_remove(wave, "Wave "))) |>
  select(-vote_first) |>
  write_rds(
    here("data", "02_processed", "eu25_partisan.rds"),
    compress = "xz"
  )
```
